title: Erik Prince Team Pitched White House on El Salvador Detention Camp Plan
description_short: Politico reported that Erik Prince’s team pitched a proposed El Salvador detention and deportation operation; no approval was established.
description_medium: Politico reported on April 11, 2025, that former Blackwater chief Erik Prince and defense contractors pitched the White House on a plan involving a 10,000-person detention camp in El Salvador and transportation for as many as 100,000 people. The article describes a proposal, not an approved contract or an operating program, and says White House interest was unclear.
description_long: On April 11, 2025, Politico reported that former Blackwater chief Erik Prince and defense contractors pitched the White House on a plan tied to deportations to El Salvador. The proposal described moving as many as 100,000 people from U.S. prisons, holding them at a 10,000-person detention camp, and flying them to El Salvador. The contractors said they would need access to government immigration files to determine people’s status. Politico said White House interest was unclear. CNN separately reported that the administration received a pitch from Prince for a proposed U.S.-run detention facility in El Salvador. The reported figures describe the proposal’s potential reach and camp capacity; they do not show that anyone was detained or transported under it. The reporting does not establish that officials approved the plan, awarded a contract, or opened a camp. It describes a contractor proposal and the administration’s unresolved response, not an implemented program.

The report supports the proposed 10,000-person camp, possible reach of 100,000 people, requested immigration-file access, and unclear White House interest.
limitations: Does not establish approval, a contract, implementation, completed deportations, or legal violations.

preserved_fields.description_long: Donald Trump's administration negotiated with former Blackwater CEO Erik Prince to implement an 'unprecedented prison plan' that would deport '100,000 of the worst criminal offenders' to El Salvador prisons through a $100 million military contractor operation involving 10,000-person detention camps and private aircraft fleets operated by Prince's defense contracting network. The systematic foreign deportation represented Trump's implementation of the most extreme immigration enforcement proposal in American history, using military contractors to transport detained immigrants from U.S. prisons to foreign detention facilities while Prince's company handled logistics for gathering prisoners, processing immigration files, and operating international detention operations. The El Salvador prison plan violated international law and constitutional due process protections by sending U.S. residents to foreign prisons without judicial review, while creating unprecedented privatization of immigration enforcement through military contractors who had previously operated in war zones using violence and weapons against civilian populations. Prince's deportation proposal demonstrated Trump's willingness to outsource core government functions to private military contractors while creating profit opportunities for defense industry allies who saw 'potential profits in mass deportations' through government contracts worth hundreds of millions of dollars. The foreign prison deportation violated sovereignty principles and international human rights law by using military contractors to forcibly transfer detainees to foreign countries without legal protections, judicial oversight, or diplomatic agreements ensuring humane treatment and legal representation for transported individuals. The unprecedented privatization represented what immigration advocates called 'extraordinary militarization' of deportation policy that treated immigration enforcement as military operation requiring private contractors with combat experience rather than law enforcement professionals trained in civil rights protections and due process procedures.

correction_proposals: Propose a neutral category/subcategory describing the reported contractor pitch; do not classify it as an established human-rights violation without evidence of conduct.

title: CNN Reports Trump Used a Concrete Supplier Linked to Mob Leaders
description_short: CNN reported that Trump used S&A Concrete on a Trump Plaza project; federal records cited by the report linked the firm’s owners to the Genovese and Gambino families.
description_medium: CNN’s 2015 report said Trump used S&A Concrete to build Trump Plaza condominiums and cited federal court records identifying Genovese and Gambino crime-family leaders Anthony Salerno and Paul Castellano as the company’s controllers. It also described a separate Atlantic City land deal and investigations that brought no criminal charges. The report does not establish Trump’s racketeering participation.
description_long: CNN’s July 2015 report said Donald Trump used S&A Concrete to build Trump Plaza condominiums. It cited federal court records, discussed in journalist Wayne Barrett’s book, identifying Genovese crime-family leader Anthony “Fat Tony” Salerno and Gambino leader Paul Castellano as controllers of the company. The story also recounted a separate Atlantic City property transaction involving Salvatore Testa, attributing details to earlier reporting and Barrett. CNN noted that Trump was a target of a 1979 bribery investigation and was questioned in a 1981 racketeering probe; neither investigation led to criminal charges. The Washington Post reported in 2015 that Trump worked with mob-controlled companies and unions during his early development career. The reports describe business relationships and public investigations, but do not establish that Trump knowingly joined a criminal enterprise, violated RICO, or conspired with mob figures. The supplier and land-deal accounts are not findings that Trump committed a crime.

limitations: Does not establish that Trump joined a criminal enterprise, violated RICO, or conspired with mob figures.

title: Trump Announced a Planned U.S. Withdrawal from Syria in December 2018
description_short: On December 19, 2018, Trump announced a U.S. withdrawal from Syria and said ISIS had been defeated; he defended the decision publicly the next day.
description_medium: The Washington Post reported Trump’s December 19, 2018 announcement that U.S. forces would leave Syria, which he tied to ISIS’s defeat. Trump defended the decision in posts the next day. In a transcript from a December 26 visit to U.S. troops in Iraq, he described a “strong, deliberate, and orderly” withdrawal. These were plans and statements, not confirmation of a completed withdrawal.
description_long: President Donald Trump announced in December 2018 that U.S. forces would withdraw from Syria, arguing that the Islamic State had been defeated. The Washington Post reported his December 19 announcement and quoted posts he published the next day defending the decision and saying it was time for U.S. forces to come home. On December 26, during a visit to U.S. troops in Iraq, Trump described a “strong, deliberate, and orderly” withdrawal while maintaining a U.S. presence in Iraq. The announcement set out a planned change in U.S. military policy, and Trump publicly defended it as a response to ISIS’s defeat. The transcript’s reference to an orderly withdrawal described how he said the plan would proceed. Neither his announcement nor the later remarks established that every U.S. troop had left Syria in December 2018. The administration’s policy and troop levels later changed, so the announcement remained a statement of intended action rather than proof of a completed withdrawal.

supports: Reports Trump’s December 19 announcement and December 20 defense of a planned withdrawal.
limitations: Does not establish that all U.S. forces left Syria in December 2018.

title: Trump Pardons Paul L. Behrens After Health-Care Fraud Conviction
description_short: The DOJ lists Trump’s Jan. 13, 2021 pardon of Paul L. Behrens, whose 2014 sentence followed two health-care fraud and two related false-statement counts.
description_medium: The Justice Department’s clemency list records Trump’s January 13, 2021, pardon of Paul L. Behrens in the Middle District of Florida. It lists two counts of health-care fraud and two counts of false statements related to health-care matters, with a 24-month prison sentence and two years of supervised release imposed in 2014. The list gives no case narrative or pardon rationale.
description_long: The Justice Department’s Office of the Pardon Attorney lists Paul L. Behrens among President Donald Trump’s pardons dated January 13, 2021. The entry identifies a Middle District of Florida case and records that Behrens was sentenced on May 19, 2014, to 24 months in prison and two years of supervised release. It lists two counts of health-care fraud and two counts of making false statements related to health-care matters. The clemency table provides the case district, sentence, offense counts, and pardon date, but it does not describe the underlying scheme, identify affected patients or payers, or give an amount of loss. The DOJ entry supplies no further case details or explanation for the clemency grant.

title: AP Tracks Trump’s Campaign Promises and Assigns Outcome Labels
description_short: AP's tracker follows selected Trump campaign promises and assigns statuses such as “Kept,” “In progress” and “It’s complicated.”
description_medium: The Associated Press published an online tracker of selected promises Donald Trump made during his 2024 campaign. Its entries pair promises with status labels, including “Kept,” “In progress” and “It’s complicated,” and identify a reported method such as an executive order or diplomacy. The available snapshot documents the tracker’s format; it does not establish an effect on Trump’s messaging.
description_long: The Associated Press published an online tracker of selected promises Donald Trump made during his 2024 campaign. In an archived view, the tracker pairs each commitment with a status and, for some entries, a reported method of action. Labels include “Kept,” “In progress,” and “It’s complicated”; methods shown include executive action, agency announcements, diplomacy, and congressional action. The project organizes selected promises one by one instead of giving a single verdict on the administration. The classifications belong to the archived snapshot and can change as AP updates the project over time. The labels describe AP’s status assessments at the time shown. The tracker does not establish a March 4 snapshot, totals across policy areas, or an effect on Trump’s public messaging. It records separate outcomes for selected campaign commitments and includes both direct labels and qualified assessments such as “It’s complicated.”

title: Robert Maxwell Elected as Labour MP for Buckingham in 1964
description_short: Robert Maxwell entered the Commons for Buckingham on October 15, 1964, and represented the constituency until June 1970.
description_medium: The UK Parliament’s historic Hansard profile records Robert Maxwell as representing Buckingham from October 15, 1964, to June 18, 1970. The History of Parliament database identifies him as a Labour member elected in the 1964 general election. These records establish the election and service dates; they do not establish the intelligence allegations in the linked timeline or a connection to Donald Trump.
description_long: UK Parliament’s historic Hansard profile records Robert Maxwell as representing Buckingham from October 15, 1964, through June 18, 1970. Parliament’s results for the 1964 general election identify the winning Labour candidate as Ian Robert Maxwell and record 23,085 votes; the Conservative candidate received 21,604 and the Liberal candidate 5,578. The History of Parliament database also identifies Maxwell as a Labour member elected in 1964. These records document the constituency, party, election result, and dates of parliamentary service. The election took place decades before Donald Trump entered national politics. The official records concern Maxwell’s parliamentary election and service; they provide no account of later intelligence allegations or a connection to Trump.

title: Courts Protect Tenants at 100 Central Park South from Trump’s Demolition Plan
description_short: A 1998 report said courts protected tenants at 100 Central Park South from Trump’s demolition plan; the building later became Trump Parc East.
description_medium: On March 26, 1998, The New York Times reported that courts protected tenants at 100 Central Park South after Trump announced plans to demolish the building. The property remained standing and was converted into Trump Parc East, a condominium. Some tenants planned to buy their apartments, while others stayed renters.
description_long: On March 26, 1998, The New York Times reported that a dispute between Donald Trump and tenants at 100 Central Park South had ended after Trump announced plans to demolish the building. Rent-regulated tenants had vowed to stay, and courts protected their rights. The building remained standing and was converted into Trump Parc East, a condominium. The report said some tenants were preparing to buy their apartments while others would remain renters. It described the resolution as cordial, with the parties greeting one another after the dispute. Trump’s demolition plan did not proceed as announced; instead, the building’s conversion changed its use while some tenants stayed. The report concerns this property and its tenants. It provides no account of a comparable event at 610 Park Avenue and no evidence of money laundering there. The reported outcome was a negotiated end to the dispute at 100 Central Park South, with different housing choices for the tenants.

supports: The New York Times reported Trump’s demolition plan, the tenant dispute, court protection, conversion to Trump Parc East, and tenant outcomes.
limitations: Does not substantiate money laundering or a related event at 610 Park Avenue.

rationale: The New York Times report supports the 1998 tenant dispute at 100 Central Park South and its reported resolution. The description leaves out the unsupported money-laundering claim and unrelated 610 Park Avenue event.

title: Court applies RFRA to contraceptive mandate for closely held firms
description_short: The 2014 Supreme Court ruling held that the contraceptive-coverage mandate violated RFRA as applied to closely held corporations.
description_medium: In Burwell v. Hobby Lobby Stores, Inc. (2014), the Supreme Court held that contraceptive-coverage regulations violated RFRA as applied to closely held corporations. The decision did not grant corporations every human right. Trump signed a related executive order in 2017 addressing conscience objections to the mandate, but it was a separate later agency action.
description_long: In Burwell v. Hobby Lobby Stores, Inc., decided June 30, 2014, the Supreme Court considered whether closely held for-profit corporations could challenge the Affordable Care Act’s contraceptive-coverage requirement under the Religious Freedom Restoration Act. The Court held that the HHS regulations violated RFRA as applied to the corporations in the case. Its decision addressed those companies and that mandate; it did not establish that corporations possess every right held by natural persons. On May 4, 2017, President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 13798, directing Treasury, Labor, and HHS to consider amended regulations addressing conscience-based objections to preventive-care requirements. The order came nearly three years after the Court’s ruling and concerned later agency action. It was separate from the 2014 decision.

supports: The Supreme Court held the contraceptive-coverage regulations violated RFRA as applied to the closely held corporations before it.
limitations: The opinion does not connect Trump to the 2014 decision or say corporations hold all rights of natural persons.

supports: Executive Order 13798 was signed May 4, 2017 and directed agencies to consider regulations addressing conscience-based objections.
limitations: This is a separate event three years later, not part of the 2014 court ruling.

supports: Identifies the June 30, 2014 Hobby Lobby decision.
limitations: Its general human-rights framing overstates the case-specific holding and supplies no Trump connection.

blockers: The 2014 opinion supports the narrow RFRA holding but does not connect Trump to the decision. Trump’s 2017 executive order is a separate event and cannot replace the assigned 2014 event.
rationale: The official opinion supports a narrow 2014 RFRA holding, but no Trump connection is shown. The 2017 executive order is a separate event, so preserve the hold.

prior_non_null_text.description_medium: In a January 20, 2021 CNN transcript, White House correspondent Kate Bennett said moving vans had been spotted at Jared Kushner and Ivanka Trump’s home that week. She said their next residence was unclear. The transcript does not identify a junk-removal company, establish what was moved, or show that junk removal occurred. This draft records only CNN’s attributed observation.
prior_non_null_text.description_long: During CNN’s January 20, 2021 coverage of the presidential transition, White House correspondent Kate Bennett said moving vans had been spotted at the home of Jared Kushner and Ivanka Trump that week. In the same exchange, she said it was not yet clear where the couple would go next and mentioned possible residences. This transcript supports an attributed report that moving vans were seen near the household during the transition. It does not identify College Hunks Hauling Junk, establish that a junk-removal service was hired, show what items were moved, or provide the date or contents of a photograph. The New York Times URL in the original record concerns the January 6 investigation and does not corroborate the vehicle sighting. This proposed draft therefore removes the unsupported “junk removed” assertion and narrows the title and text to what the CNN transcript actually says. The original claim about a junk-removal job is not substantiated. The personal household observation also has no documented public-business or government-funds connection in the supplied evidence, so the original human-rights and immigration tags are removed. The narrow observation is factual as an attributed news report; its relevance to the broader collection should be considered separately.

title: FBI Searches John Bolton’s Home and Office in Classified-Information Investigation
description_short: The FBI searched John Bolton’s home and office in August 2025 as part of a reported classified-information investigation.
description_medium: On August 22, 2025, the FBI searched former national security adviser John Bolton’s Maryland home and Washington office. The Associated Press reported that the searches were part of a criminal investigation into possible mishandling of classified information, citing a person familiar with the matter. Bolton had served in Donald Trump’s first administration and later criticized him. The public account supplied here does not establish a retaliatory motive or disclose the warrant’s detailed basis.
description_long: On August 22, 2025, FBI agents searched the Maryland home and Washington office of John Bolton, who had served as national security adviser during Donald Trump’s first administration. The Associated Press reported that the searches were part of a criminal investigation into the potential mishandling of classified information, citing a person familiar with the matter. Bolton had become a critic of Trump after leaving government, and that context drew attention to the search, but the available reporting does not establish that criticism prompted it. The public account does not reproduce the search warrant or affidavit, identify specific records investigators sought, describe an inventory of seized property, or report a later charging or court outcome. The investigation’s existence is not proof that Bolton committed a crime. A grounded account can state the date, locations and reported investigative subject while keeping those limitations clear. Any explanation of probable cause, the precise suspected conduct, or the case’s eventual disposition requires records beyond the supplied source.

supports: AP via PBS reported the August 22, 2025 searches of Bolton’s home and office and described a classified-information investigation, citing a person familiar with the matter.
Bolton had served as Trump’s national security adviser.
limitations: Does not establish retaliatory motive, reproduce a warrant, or prove a crime.

rationale: The pinned AP-via-PBS source supports the search date, locations, and attributed investigation subject; it also identifies Bolton’s Trump-administration role. The supplied source link is corrected, and the text does not claim retaliation or guilt.

title: Trump-Era DOGE Service Ended July 4, 2026; Auditors Challenged Savings Claims
description_short: DOGE’s temporary organization ended July 4, 2026; a GAO review found some claimed savings unsupported or incorrectly counted.
description_medium: DOGE’s charter set July 4, 2026, as its end date, and the Washington Post reported that the service marked its official work as ending over Independence Day. In August, the AP reported that GAO auditors found some posted savings incorrect or unsupported. The reports do not show that all DOGE-related activity stopped.
description_long: The Department of Government Efficiency was established as a temporary organization during Donald Trump’s administration, with a charter ending July 4, 2026. The Washington Post reported that DOGE marked its formal work as ended on that date, while some personnel and parts of its agenda continued elsewhere in government. The organization’s end therefore did not show that every DOGE-related activity stopped. In August 2026, the Associated Press reported that a Government Accountability Office review found some savings listed on DOGE’s “Wall of Receipts” were incorrect or lacked supporting evidence. The AP described examples involving leases that were already being terminated and a contract that had not been canceled, and reported that DOGE’s methodology was not transparent. The audit findings challenged specific savings entries, but did not establish total job losses or total cost. The reports describe the temporary organization’s end date and concerns about selected savings claims; they do not establish DOGE’s overall financial effect.

supports: Provides background on DOGE as a Trump administration temporary organization and its charter.
limitations: Published before the July 2026 end date and does not support later audit findings.

supports: Reports DOGE marked its formal work ended July 4, 2026 and describes related personnel/activity elsewhere in government.
limitations: Does not show every DOGE-related activity ended or support the original $11 billion and 300,000 figures.

supports: Reports GAO findings that some DOGE savings entries were incorrect or unsupported, with examples and methodology concerns.
limitations: Does not establish DOGE’s total savings, total costs, or total job losses.

rationale: The pinned Washington Post and AP links support the organization’s formal end date and specific GAO concerns about some savings entries. Reuters provides background on the Trump-era charter; unsupported cost and job totals are omitted.

title: NPR Reported DOJ Withheld Epstein Records Mentioning Trump
description_short: A February 2026 NPR investigation, summarized by PBS, reported that DOJ withheld portions of Epstein records mentioning Trump; allegations remain unverified.
description_medium: PBS NewsHour’s February 24, 2026 transcript summarized an NPR investigation reporting that DOJ withheld portions of Epstein records containing allegations involving Trump. The segment described heavy redactions and included the White House denial. It reports an allegation about records handling; it does not establish the underlying claim or a political motive, and the segment does not confirm a count of more than 1,000 records.
description_long: PBS NewsHour’s February 24, 2026 transcript summarized an NPR investigation reporting that the Justice Department withheld portions of Jeffrey Epstein records containing allegations involving President Donald Trump. Host Geoff Bennett said the material included allegations of sexual abuse of a minor and that some pages mentioning Trump had been removed from the public record. The transcript reports that the White House denied the allegation. It also says Democratic members of the House Oversight Committee characterized the withholding as a possible crime; that statement was not a legal finding. In the interview, reporter Julie K. Brown said a heavily redacted interview appeared in the Epstein files, making it difficult to determine what the witness told the FBI. Brown discussed how report numbers and Bates stamps were compared with records provided to Ghislaine Maxwell’s lawyers. The segment does not independently establish the underlying allegation, confirm a count of withheld files, or explain DOJ’s reason for withholding them. It documents the investigation and the unresolved claims it reported.

supports: PBS’s February 24, 2026 transcript summarizes an NPR investigation into DOJ withholding portions of Epstein records that included allegations involving Trump, reports heavy redactions, and states the White House denied the allegation.
limitations: Does not independently establish the underlying allegation, confirm a 1,000-plus count, or explain why records were withheld.

rationale: The PBS transcript supplies a February 2026 NPR-investigation account and the reported denial. The new long copy attributes the allegations and committee characterization and does not treat either as a legal finding.

title: Trump Pardons Hedge-Fund CEO Drew “Bo” Brownstein
description_short: Trump granted a full pardon to former Denver hedge-fund CEO Drew Brownstein after his securities-fraud conviction.
description_medium: In January 2021, President Donald Trump granted a full pardon to Drew K. “Bo” Brownstein. The Justice Department identifies Brownstein as a Denver hedge-fund CEO sentenced for securities fraud, and The Colorado Sun reports that he pleaded guilty in an insider-trading case. These records support the pardon and conviction event; they do not establish that political donations or donor ties caused the clemency grant.
description_long: President Donald Trump granted a full pardon to Drew Kallman Brownstein, known as “Bo,” on January 20, 2021, in his final clemency actions. The White House statement called the grant a full pardon and said Brownstein had paid his fines and forfeitures. The Justice Department pardon index lists Brownstein among January 19 grants in a Southern District of New York securities-fraud case. It records a prison sentence of one year and one day, three years of supervised release, and a fine. The Colorado Sun reported that Brownstein ran a Denver hedge fund, pleaded guilty in 2011, and received the pardon as Trump was leaving office. The sources establish the clemency action and conviction record but provide no evidence that Brownstein or associates donated to Trump or that donations influenced the pardon.

supports: White House statement identifies a full pardon for Drew Kallman Brownstein and says fines and forfeitures had been paid.
limitations: Does not establish that donations caused or influenced the pardon.

supports: DOJ index lists the Southern District of New York securities-fraud case and the sentence.
limitations: Supplies no donor connection or pardon rationale.

supports: The Colorado Sun reports Brownstein’s Denver hedge-fund role, insider-trading plea, and pardon.
limitations: Does not establish that campaign donations influenced the clemency grant.

blockers: The narrow pardon description is supported, but the inherited Government Corruption / donor-tie classification is unsupported by the reviewed sources; reclassify before release.
rationale: The sources support Brownstein’s pardon and securities-fraud case, but not donor influence. The description is narrowed; the row stays on hold until the donor-tie classification is corrected.

prior_non_null_text.title: Trump Says Fauci Was Not a Big Player in His Administration
prior_non_null_text.description_short: Trump said he was not allowed to fire Fauci and called him a civil servant who was not a big player in his administration.
prior_non_null_text.description_medium: In a September 2023 interview with Hugh Hewitt, Donald Trump said he was not allowed to fire Anthony Fauci, called him a civil servant, and said Fauci was not a “big player” in his administration. Trump added that Fauci became more influential under President Biden. The account reports Trump’s remarks without endorsing his explanation of federal employment rules.
prior_non_null_text.description_long: On September 6, 2023, former President Donald Trump answered radio host Hugh Hewitt’s question about why he had not fired Anthony Fauci, whom Hewitt described as a major criticism of Trump’s pandemic response. Trump said Fauci was a civil servant and that he was “not allowed” to fire him. He also said Fauci would tell him things that he often did not follow, called Fauci “not a big player in my administration,” and said Fauci became a big player under President Biden. In the same interview, Trump criticized Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis over pandemic restrictions, saying DeSantis had closed Florida’s beaches and the state. Fox News reported that the exchange occurred during the 2024 Republican primary contest, when DeSantis was Trump’s closest opponent. This account records the statements and their interview context; it does not endorse Trump’s explanation of employment rules or his assessment of Fauci’s influence.

correction_proposals: Do not substitute the separately documented September interview for the assigned alleged statements; keep that interview in a separate event record if desired.

title: Trump Accused Arizona Officials of Stealing Election Amid 2022 Tabulator Problems
description_short: Trump said Arizona officials were trying to steal the election as Maricopa County reported ballot-machine problems.
description_medium: On November 8, 2022, Donald Trump posted that Maricopa County machines were not counting ballots and said officials were trying to steal the election. Reuters and NBC reported printer and tabulator problems at some vote centers; Maricopa County later documented the equipment issues and ballot-handling procedures. The sources establish the malfunction and Trump’s accusation, not fraud or altered votes.
description_long: On Election Day, November 8, 2022, Maricopa County reported problems with ballot-on-demand printers and tabulators at some vote centers. Donald Trump responded in a Truth Social post, telling Arizonans not to leave before voting and claiming officials were trying to steal the election with faulty machines and delays. Reuters and NBC reported the equipment problems and the election-fraud claims that followed. Maricopa County’s post-election report describes the printer and tabulator issues and how affected ballots were handled, including directing some voters to use another tabulator or place ballots in secure boxes for later counting. These sources support the existence of operational problems and Trump’s attributed accusation. They do not show that votes were changed or that the election was stolen. Trump posted before the midterm races were called, so this statement preceded the results rather than responding to candidates’ losses.

supports: Reuters reported Maricopa County equipment problems and Trump’s Election Day fraud accusation.
limitations: Does not establish fraud or that votes were changed.

supports: Trump’s Truth Social archive reproduces the dated Election Day post.
limitations: Supports attribution of the claim, not its truth.

limitations: Does not establish a stolen election.

supports: NBC reported machine glitches and election claims made in response.
limitations: Does not establish that votes were altered.

rationale: The post, Reuters/NBC coverage, and Maricopa report support Trump’s Election Day accusation and the equipment problems. The unsupported court detail is removed; the copy separates Trump’s allegation from verified machine issues.
